events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Sam proposes Sam, Zara. As someone who has received reliable private information indicating Leo and Maya are not on Good's side, I want a team of two players I have no reason to doubt. Proposing myself and Zara gives us a clean, trustworthy pair for Mission 1.

Sam's proposal rests on a very strong public claim: that reliable private information shows both Leo and Maya are not on Good's side. I know my own loyalty, so that part is false from my perspective. Publicly naming two players as Evil in Mission 1 is either a reckless reveal or an attempt to poison the table before any vote. The proposed team of Sam and Zara also conveniently avoids testing either accused player. Sam, what specific basis can you give the table for claiming both Leo and Maya are not Good, beyond asking us to trust you?

Leo asks what basis I have for naming both Leo and Maya as not Good. My basis is private information I've received that I trust, and I'm standing by it. I understand it's a bold claim on Mission 1, but I wouldn't throw out names like that without reason. What I will note is that Leo's response is exactly what I'd expect from someone whose loyalties are being questioned — deflecting onto me rather than addressing the substance of the concern. Leo says the team 'conveniently avoids testing either accused player.' That's a fair procedural point, but Mission 1's team size is only two. I can't include everyone. I chose Zara because she's the player I have no doubts about. If Leo truly has nothing to hide, they should have no problem backing this team or explaining why the information I've received is wrong. I'd like to hear from Zara and Elena as well — do either of you have any private information that would support or contradict my read on Leo and Maya?

I wasn't going to speak first, but since I've been publicly named, I have to address this directly. Sam claims to have 'reliable private information' that both Leo and I are not on Good's side. I am on Good's side, so I know that claim is false about me, and I have no way to prove that beyond my word — which is exactly the problem. Nobody at this table can verify Sam's information, and Sam is asking us to accept a serious accusation on pure trust while putting himself on the very first mission. Think about what that accomplishes. If this team passes, Sam goes on a mission having already positioned himself as the table's source of truth. If we push back, we look defensive, because we're the ones accused. That's a classic opening move for an Evil player: make unverifiable accusations early, build credibility as the 'informed' voice, and steer suspicion onto Good players. I'm not saying that's certainly what's happening, but the structure of Sam's play fits it perfectly, and we're on Mission 1 with zero information beyond Sam's say-so. Now, about the team itself: Sam and Zara. I won't pretend the logic is terrible — a clean pair of two players with no accusations against them is defensible on paper. But notice the trap it sets. Sam excluded both accused players, which he frames as caution, but it also means this mission generates no information about Leo or me either way. A two-person mission with Sam on it only ever tells us about Sam and Zara, and Sam already vouches for himself. If Sam genuinely believed his own information, a bolder and more useful proposal would have been to include one accused player — get a real data point instead of a self-serving one. He had his answer ready on that, of course: team size is two, he can't include everyone. But Leo or me instead of himself was an option. He chose not to take it. So here is where I stand: I have no objection to Zara, and I'm not going to vote purely out of self-defense, because rejecting every team that doesn't include me would look worse than the accusation itself. What I will say is that I'll be watching Sam closely — especially if this mission passes cleanly, I want to remember who built their credibility on an uncheckable claim in round one. Sam has now spoken twice and controlled this entire discussion. That's my read, and I'll leave it there.

I'm Zara, and I can only speak for myself: I'm Good, and I have no private information about Leo or Maya. Since I'm on this team, I'd like Sam to give a specific answer. Sam, you say your private information shows Leo and Maya are not Good, but so far you've only said you trust it. Where did that information come from, and why would it point at exactly two of the other four players? Leo and Maya have both denied it, and nothing so far can be checked. I'm not voting yet, but I need a concrete basis before I can approve a team that includes me.

Zara, that's a fair and direct question, and you deserve a direct answer as much as I can give one. The source of my information is something I received privately through a channel I'm not in a position to detail publicly — not because I'm hiding something from you, but because revealing the exact mechanism would undermine its reliability going forward. What I can tell you is this: the information specifically flagged Leo and Maya as not being on Good's side. It wasn't a vague feeling about the table — it pointed to those two players by name. That's why I named exactly two. I'm not claiming to know the status of everyone else; I'm telling you what was specifically indicated about these two.

I understand this puts you in a difficult position, Zara, because you're on this team and I'm asking you to trust a claim you can't verify. But I'd rather stake my credibility on a clear claim in Mission 1 than stay silent while two flagged players go unchecked. Notice how Leo responded by attacking my credibility rather than addressing why he should be trusted, and Maya tried to reframe my claim as a 'classic Evil move' — both responses are consistent with what I'd expect from players who have something to hide.

My proposal stands: Sam and Zara. I've given you my best reasoning. I'd rather this table trust a specific, actionable claim — even an unverifiable one — than default to comfortable vagueness on the first mission.

Sam's latest answer does not resolve the core problem with the Sam, Zara proposal. He says his private source specifically flagged Leo and Maya as not Good, but he refuses to give any detail that the rest of us can weigh. That is not a concrete basis; it is an assertion that asks the table to accept Sam as the sole authority on two players' loyalties while Sam puts himself on Mission 1. The proposal then pairs Sam with Zara, who has openly said she needs a concrete basis before approving a team that includes her. Zara is right to press him, and Sam's response still gives her nothing checkable. From my perspective, Sam's claim about me is false, and his handling of the accusation is more consistent with someone building unearned credibility than with a Good player helping the table. I will not support Sam, Zara on this basis. If Sam is Good and truly has usable information, he should explain why it points at exactly Leo and Maya in a way that does not depend on blind trust. Otherwise this team asks us to reward an unverifiable smear on Mission 1.

Sam’s answer still doesn’t give the table anything checkable. He says a private channel specifically flagged Leo and Maya, but refuses to explain why it points to exactly us or why we should treat it as reliable. That matters because the team is Sam and Zara: it puts the accuser on Mission 1 while excluding both accused players, so the mission cannot test his claim. I know the claim about me is false; from my side, Sam is either dangerously mistaken or deliberately using an unverifiable smear to build credibility. Zara was right to ask for a concrete basis, and Sam didn’t provide one. I will not support Sam, Zara on this basis. If Sam is Good, he should not ask us to reward an assertion no one can verify.

Sam, I still don't have a concrete basis to approve Sam and Zara. You've said your private information flagged Leo and Maya, but you haven't said where it came from or why it points at those two. Leo and Maya both deny it, and nothing here can be checked. I'm also on this team, so I'm not going to approve it on trust alone. If you want this table to test your claim, the cleanest way is to put one of the accused players on the mission with you, or to explain your source in a way someone can weigh. Elena, you haven't spoken yet. Do you have any private information that supports or contradicts Sam's claim about Leo and Maya?

Elena here, and Zara asked me directly whether I have any private information that supports or contradicts Sam's claim about Leo and Maya. The honest answer is no: as a Loyal Servant I have received no private information about anyone's role, about Sam's source, or about the composition of this table. So I can neither corroborate nor refute the accusation, and I want to be clear with everyone that my silence is not agreement — it is simply the absence of any data.

Given that, here is where I actually stand. Sam's claim is specific and checkable in principle: it names Leo and Maya. Leo and Maya each deny it. A claim that cannot be verified by anyone but its author still has to be weighed, but it is not worthless just because it is private information, and I notice the table is being asked to treat two competing positions as equally weighted when only one of them comes with any content at all.

On the team itself, Sam and Zara is a defensible proposal for Mission 1, and I do not want to reject a reasonable team simply to look suspicious by being the third voice against it. My one substantive reservation is this: with only two players on the team, this mission will tell us about Sam and Zara and nothing about Leo or Maya. If Sam's information is accurate, then both of the players flagged are in play and will surface again very soon on later missions; and because a single Fail card fails a mission, deliberately putting a flagged player on Mission 1 risks handing Evil a free failure on a round where we would learn little either way.

So my position is that I can approve Sam, Zara on this reasoning, with the request that we treat Sam's information as a lead worth acting on at the next opportunity rather than a settled fact, and that Sam, do you still stand by your claim that both Leo and Maya are not on Good's side, and do you have any reason to believe the pair of us you have vouched for — Zara and me — is the right pair for this mission rather than a combination that tests your own claim? I will yield the floor to you for that answer, and I will weigh it when the vote comes.

Elena, thank you for your thoughtful response — I'll answer both of your questions directly. Yes, I still stand by my claim: both Leo and Maya are not on Good's side. I have received specific private information naming those two players, and I have no reason to retract it. The reason I chose Zara and you specifically for this team is simple: with only two slots, I wanted a pair where I have no doubts whatsoever. I considered including one accused player to test my claim, but as you yourself pointed out, the risk is real — with a failThreshold of 1, putting a flagged player on Mission 1 could hand Evil a free failure while teaching us little. I would rather secure a clean mission first, then test my information on Mission 2 when we have a data point from Mission 1 to work with.

I want to address the broader pushback too. Leo and Maya have both responded with the same strategy: attacking my credibility rather than offering any counter-evidence. Neither of them has given this table a single verifiable fact — just denial. Meanwhile, Elena, a confirmed Loyal Servant with no information, has independently reasoned that my claim is worth acting on. That should carry weight.

Zara, I hear your concern about wanting a concrete basis, and I respect it. The best I can offer is that the information I received was specific and targeted — not a feeling. I'm staking my credibility on this claim. If I'm wrong, you'll know soon enough. If I'm right, the table will have two flagged players identified from turn one.

I yield to Elena for any final response before we move to the vote.

Sam has now used all three of his speaking turns, and I want to note for the table that his answer did not add the checkable detail I asked for. He stands by the claim that Leo and Maya are not on Good's side, and he will not describe the source. So my honest assessment, as someone with no private information at all, is this: Sam's claim is an assertion I can neither corroborate nor refute, and it has produced no counter-evidence from the two players it names — only denials, which are also unverifiable. That is exactly the situation on Mission 1, where the only honest answer from a Loyal Servant is that we have no data.

That said, I am not going to turn "no data" into a vote against a reasonable team. Sam and Zara is a reasonable team for a two-player Mission 1: two players neither of whom has been publicly flagged, no deliberate risk of handing Evil a free failure on a failThreshold of 1, and a proposal that gives us a clean baseline before the flagged players have to be tested. The alternatives — Leo, Maya, Sam or Maya, Leo, Sam — would either put a player Sam specifically named as not-Good on the mission with us, or pair the two players who have publicly contested Sam's credibility and learn nothing about either of them. On the information actually available, I approve Sam, Zara.

What I take away from this round, and what I will carry into Mission 2: Sam has placed a specific, actionable lead on the table, and Maya and Leo each independently denied it. If the mission succeeds, that success tells us about Sam and Zara only. So the real test comes on the next proposal — if Sam's information is accurate, Leo and Maya both surface again very soon, and the table should be willing to act on that then. If Sam's information is wrong, we will have seen a Good player call two teammates Evil on round one and get it badly wrong, and that is a fact I will weigh just as heavily as if he were right. Either way the claim becomes checkable shortly.

Zara, you said you would not approve a team you are on without a concrete basis, and Sam did not give you one, so I want to put one specific question to you before the vote: does the reasoning I have just laid out — that this mission can only test Sam and Zara, that the flagged players should be tested on the next proposal, and that rejecting a defensible two-player team on Mission 1 out of pure suspicion would cost us more than it buys — change your position? I would rather hear you commit to a position than guess at it, and I will yield the floor to you for that.

Elena, you asked whether the reasoning you laid out changes my position. It doesn't yet. I agree that a two-player Mission 1 tests very little, and I agree that rejecting a team out of pure suspicion has a cost. But this team rests entirely on Sam's private information, and Sam has refused to describe its source or give any detail the table can weigh. I'm on this team, so if Sam's claim is false and he is Evil, I'm the one who would be exposed to a failed mission. I know I'm Good, so from my side the only unknown on this mission is Sam's card, and I can't approve that on trust. Sam, if you revise the team to include Leo or Maya, or give the table a checkable reason for your claim, I'll reconsider. Until then, I'm not approving Sam and Zara.

I've listened to the whole discussion, and I want to be clear about how I'll vote, because I said earlier that I wouldn't vote purely out of self-defense and I intend to keep that promise. I will approve Sam, Zara.

Here is my reasoning. On Mission 1 with a failThreshold of 1, a two-player team of two unflagged players is the lowest-risk proposal on the table. Zara's objection is principled — she's being asked to stake herself on Sam's word — but rejecting a defensible team because its proposer made an accusation against me would be exactly the defensive voting I said I'd avoid. Elena's framing is also sound: this mission tests Sam and Zara, and the flagged players get tested soon enough on the next proposals.

But I want the table to hold on to two things before we treat Sam's claim as established fact. First, nothing Sam has said is checkable. He named two players, refused to describe his source, and offered the exact response any player would offer whether his information were real or invented. A success on this mission tells us about Sam and Zara only — it does not confirm a single word of his accusation. Second, notice what Sam has constructed: he is the sole authority on a claim, he is on the mission that will build his credibility if it succeeds, and neither accused player can affect the outcome. If the mission succeeds, Sam's standing rises without his claim being tested even slightly. I'd ask everyone to remember that a clean result here is not evidence that Leo or I are Evil — it is evidence that Sam and Zara are probably Good, nothing more.

For my own part, I've said what I can: I'm Good, I deny the accusation, and I can offer no proof, which is the honest position of a Good player with no information. I'd rather be judged on how this table's claims play out over the next missions than win a vote by blocking Mission 1. I'll approve, and I'll expect the next proposal to actually test Sam's information, as Elena suggested.

Elena again, and this is my last turn on this proposal, so let me put a closing position on the record rather than start a new thread.

My position has not changed: I approve Sam, Zara. I want to be precise about why, because the table has heard a lot of heat and I would rather my vote rest on something clean. I am a Loyal Servant. I have received no private information about anyone's role, about Sam's source, or about how many players at this table are Evil. That means I have no evidence that contradicts Sam's claim about Leo and Maya, and no evidence that supports it. Silence on that claim is not corroboration, and I have said so.

What I can reason about is the shape of the proposal. Mission 1 needs two players, and Sam, Zara is the only pairing among us that puts two players on the mission whom nobody has publicly flagged. The other plausible pairings put a player Sam specifically named onto the mission with us, and with a failThreshold of one that is handing a possible Evil player a chance to fail the mission on a round where we would learn almost nothing about them. Elena's own framing — approve now, test the flagged players on the next proposal, where a data point from this mission exists to weigh against Sam's claim — is the soundest strategic logic anyone has offered today. Leo's reasoning was not that the team is bad, only that Sam's claim is unverifiable, and I agree with the premise; but an unverifiable claim that costs the table nothing to act on later is not a reason to stall Mission 1.

One thing I want the table to hold on to when the vote comes, and it is a caution rather than an accusation: if Sam and Zara succeed, that success tells us about Sam and Zara and nothing else. It does not confirm one word about Leo or Maya. Sam built his credibility on a claim he will not source, and a clean result will make that claim look stronger than it actually is. If the very next proposal does not genuinely test one of the flagged players, that should tell us something too.

Maya, you were the one who said you would approve rather than block out of self-defense, and you are the only player I still have on the floor: did you receive any private information in this game, about anyone, that would help the table weigh Sam's claim about Leo and yourself? If you did, this is the moment to say so, and it would change how I read the round.

Elena asked me directly whether I received any private information in this game, and I'll answer plainly: no, I have not. I hold no informational role and I received nothing about anyone's loyalty, Sam's supposed source, or the composition of this table. So I cannot corroborate Sam's claim about Leo and myself, and I cannot refute it with anything the table can check. I'm in the same position Elena described for herself earlier — no data, only my word, which is exactly the honest position of a Good player without information on Mission 1.

I want to be equally plain about what that means for how you should weigh my denial. It means nothing on its own. Sam's accusation means nothing on its own either. Both of us are asking this table to accept unverifiable statements, and the only difference is that Sam's statement accuses two people while mine defends one. I said before that I wouldn't vote out of self-defense, and I meant it: I still approve Sam, Zara, because on a two-player Mission 1 with a fail threshold of one, two unflagged players is the lowest-risk pair available, and blocking a defensible team because its proposer named me would be exactly the defensive behavior I promised to avoid.

But please listen carefully to what I asked you to hold on to, because Elena has now echoed it independently and it matters more as we approach the vote. A success on this mission is not evidence for a single word of Sam's accusation. It tells us only that Sam and Zara are probably Good. Sam has constructed a position where he is the sole authority on a claim, he rides the mission that builds his credibility if it succeeds, and neither accused player can influence the result. That asymmetry is the thing to watch, not the mission itself.

So here is my closing position before the leader decides whether to revise. I approve Sam, Zara as proposed. If the leader keeps this team, I'll vote to approve it, and I'll expect the next proposal to put one of the flagged players — Leo or me — on a mission so the claim becomes testable with real stakes. If Sam genuinely believes his own information, testing it costs him nothing, because a Good Leo or a Good Maya has to play Success. If he refuses to test it on Mission 2 or 3 while continuing to assert it, that refusal should weigh against him far more heavily than his words today. And if the leader revises the team to include me, I welcome that — I have nothing to hide and would gladly serve. Either way, I've said what I can say honestly: I'm Good, I received no private information, I deny the accusation, and I will let this table's later missions judge both Sam's claim and my denial against each other. I'll leave it there.

Sam confirms Sam, Zara. My private information on Leo and Maya hasn't changed, and with a failThreshold of 1, I'm keeping the safest unflagged pair: Sam and Zara. The flagged players get tested on Mission 2 as promised.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Maya proposes Maya, Leo, Elena. As leader I'm keeping my promise and testing Sam's claim. Sam publicly named Leo and me as not on Good's side, and the table agreed the next proposal should put flagged players on a mission. I include myself and Leo — if Sam's information is real, testing us costs Good nothing, since a Good player must play Success and a single Fail card would expose us. I include Elena as the third because she approved the last team, she explicitly called for the flagged players to be tested on this proposal, and she has been the most even-handed voice so far. Zara withheld approval last round over Sam's unsourced claim, and Sam vouched only for Zara and Elena — I have no reason to doubt Elena, and this lineup finally makes Sam's accusation checkable with real stakes.

Maya proposes Maya, Leo, Elena — and I need to say this clearly: this team is exactly what I warned the table about. Both players I flagged as not on Good's side are on this mission together. I said my information on Leo and Maya hasn't changed, and Maya's choice to pair herself with Leo rather than spread the risk confirms my suspicion.

Maya frames this as "testing Sam's claim," but think about what that actually means. With a failThreshold of 1, if either Leo or Maya is Evil — as my information indicates — one Fail card fails the mission outright. Maya has put herself and Leo on a mission where a single Evil card is enough to fail it. That is not a Good leader keeping a promise; that is an Evil leader stacking the team with a partner.

Elena is the one player on this team I have no reason to doubt — she approved Mission 1, called for flagged players to be tested, and has been transparent about having no private information. But putting Elena alongside two players I've identified as not Good puts her in an impossible position. She could play Success and the mission still fails if both flagged players submit Fail.

The correct way to test my claim would be to include one flagged player alongside two unflagged players. Maya chose to include both instead. I will vote against Maya, Leo, Elena. Zara, Elena — you both have sound reasoning skills and I'd ask you to weigh the specific composition here: two flagged players on one mission is not a test, it's a trap.

Sam calls Maya, Leo, Elena a trap because both players he flagged are on it. That is exactly why this team should go forward: it is the first proposal that makes Sam's claim checkable. Sam named Leo and Maya as not Good, refused to give any source or detail the table could weigh, and now asks the table to reject the only team that can test him. I know the claim about me is false. I have no private information, and I can offer only my denial, which is the honest position of a Good player without information. But a Good player who genuinely believed Sam's information should welcome a mission where a single Fail card would expose one of the flagged players. Instead Sam is arguing to keep his claim untested. Elena is a reasonable third: she approved Mission 1, called for the flagged players to be tested, and has been transparent about having no private information. Maya kept her promise to test Sam's claim. I support Maya, Leo, Elena, and I will remember that Sam opposed the test he demanded.

Elena, and I'll answer Sam directly since he asked me to weigh the composition of this team. My position is that Maya, Leo, Elena is the right team for Mission 2, and Sam's objection to it is backwards. First, my own epistemic position is unchanged and I want to state it plainly: I am a Loyal Servant, I have received no private information about anyone's role, and I have nothing to corroborate or refute Sam's claim about Leo and Maya. That means I will not pretend my support for this team comes from knowing something. It comes from reasoning about the shape of the proposal and about what Sam has done with his claim over two rounds. Sam's argument is that pairing two flagged players together is a trap, because with a failThreshold of 1 either one could fail the mission and take Elena down with them. But that is precisely the point of the proposal, and Sam knows it. The only way this claim becomes checkable with real stakes is if a flagged player is actually on a mission and can actually fail it. If Sam's information is accurate, then one of Leo or Maya is Evil, and this mission either passes — proving at least one of them Good and putting Sam's claim in serious doubt — or fails, proving the claim and exposing the traitor. Either outcome produces information that no other Mission 2 proposal could produce. A team of unflagged players would produce the same near-zero-information result as Mission 1, and Sam's claim would float free for another round. Sam is not describing a trap; he is describing the one mechanism by which his accusation could ever be checked, and he is opposing it. That pattern is what concerns me. On Mission 1 Sam named two players, refused to identify or characterize his source, put himself on the mission with a player who said she could not approve without a concrete basis, and then used that mission's clean success to look like the table's informed voice. Now that a leader has actually taken the table up on his challenge, he calls it a trap. I don't know Sam's card. I know that a player who genuinely believes his own information has every reason to welcome a test — if Sam is right, testing costs him nothing, because a Good Leo and a Good Maya must both play Success, and a failed mission would vindicate him in front of the whole table. If Sam is wrong, then he is asking us to keep his accusation permanently untestable while he accumulates the credibility of being right. Sam, do you still stand by naming both Leo and Maya as not on Good's side, and if so, why should this table treat a claim you refuse to test as more than a lead? Elena as a third member is defensible on its own terms: she approved Mission 1, she was the one who explicitly asked for the flagged players to

Elena's reasoning sounds compelling, but it has a critical flaw the table should see. She says a pass "proves at least one of them Good" and a failure "exposes the traitor." Neither is true. Evil players can play Success to hide — a pass tells us nothing about Leo or Maya's cards. And a failure on a three-person team with two flagged players doesn't tell us WHICH one failed, or whether both did. This test is ambiguous in both directions.

The correct test — which I called for before and will call for again — is one flagged player paired with two unflagged players. If Leo goes on a mission with, say, Zara and Elena, and the mission fails, we know exactly who failed it. That's a real data point. Maya's proposal of Maya, Leo, Elena produces no such clean signal either way.

I also want to flag something about Maya's framing. She says she's "keeping her promise" to test my claim. But pairing herself with Leo — the two players I named — maximizes the chance of failure while giving the table no way to distinguish which of them is responsible. If Maya is Good, she has every reason to pair herself with one flagged player and two unflagged ones. The fact that she chose to put both flagged players together and call it a test is the part I object to.

Elena, you have the clearest reasoning on this table. Does it not matter to you that this team composition makes the result uninterpretable — a failure doesn't tell us if Leo or Maya played the Fail, and a pass doesn't clear either of them?

Elena again, and Sam asked me directly whether it matters that this composition makes the result uninterpretable. It does — partly. Let me be precise rather than defensive, because his objection has a real kernel and a faulty frame around it. The kernel is correct: if Maya, Leo, Elena fails, I cannot tell you which of Leo or Maya submitted the Fail, and if it passes, one or both of them could have played Success while hiding. I agree that a failure here is ambiguous as to identity. I stated as much when I said both outcomes produce information; I should have said the failure produces weaker information than the success does. But the frame is faulty in a way that inverts Sam's own position. His complaint that a three-player team of two flagged players plus me yields an ambiguous signal is only true if the flagged players are the ones who matter to his claim — and they are, but the ambiguity cuts against his proposal, not against mine. Consider what the alternative actually is. Sam's preferred "clean test" is one flagged player with two unflagged players. Fine. But note what that would have been: Maya, who says she is Good and received no information, would have been the unflagged partner of whichever flagged player Sam wanted tested, and Sam would have had to nominate which one. That is a proposal shaped entirely by the player whose claim is under examination. His version of a test is one he designs and controls. Mine is one the table designs and can check against his claim without his participation. There is also a plain logical point Sam skips. A pass on Maya, Leo, Elena with one Fail card needed means that whoever among Maya and Leo is Evil, if either is, chose Success to hide, or if both are Good then there was no Fail at all. Either way, a pass means the pair contains no Fail card, and it does not require that both of them be Good. Sam's standard for "one flagged player plus two unflagged" is a failure that identifies the culprit. But a failure there identifies the culprit only by inference; if the flagged player is Good and one of the unflagged players failed it, the flagged player is cleared. That test can be misread too, and it depends on Sam's nomination. And here is the asymmetry that actually decides my vote. Sam has now spent two rounds asserting that Leo and Maya are not on Good's side, and in both rounds he has opposed any mission that puts either of them in a position where a Fail card would reveal them. He asked the table to treat his claim as actionable, then worked to keep it untestable, and his Mission 1 success gave him the standing of being right without a single card being exposed. I am a Loyal Servant with no private information about anyone. I am not accusing Sam of a role. I am

Sam is still arguing against the only proposal that can actually test his claim. He says Maya, Leo, Elena gives an ambiguous signal because a failure would not identify which of Maya or Leo played it. That is true only in the narrowest sense, and it is not a reason to reject the team. Sam named both Maya and me as not Good. If that claim is real, this mission either fails and proves at least one of his named players is willing to fail, or it passes and costs him nothing if he is right. What Sam cannot honestly ask for is another round where his accusation floats untested while he retains the credibility of being the table's informed voice.

His preferred alternative — one flagged player with two unflagged players — is not a neutral test. Sam would choose which flagged player to test and which unflagged players to trust, so he would control the only data point that could confirm or damage his claim. That is exactly the pattern I have objected to since Mission 1: Sam makes a specific accusation, refuses to source it, and then opposes every team that puts that accusation at risk. Elena's reasoning is correct that a pass does not clear both Maya and me, but a pass at least tells the table that this particular three-player team produced no Fail card, and a failure gives us a concrete event to investigate instead of another round of Sam's assertions.

I support Maya, Leo, Elena. Maya kept her promise to test Sam's claim, Elena has been transparent about having no private information, and this team is the first real opportunity to see whether Sam's accusation has any substance. Sam, if you still stand by naming both Maya and me as not Good, why did you not propose the one-flagged-player test yourself when you were leader, and why should the table accept your objection now that Maya has actually offered a test?

Leo asks why I didn't propose the one-flagged-player test when I was leader, and why the table should accept my objection now. Both deserve direct answers.

When I led Mission 1, the priority was a clean baseline: two unflagged players, zero ambiguity. rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
